steps.observation: You have 60 seconds. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Key differences between DNA and RNA  

1. Sugar  
   • DNA: deoxyribose (lacks an ‑OH on the 2′ carbon).  
   • RNA: ribose (has an ‑OH on the 2′ carbon).

2. Bases  
   • DNA: adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C), guanine (G).  
   • RNA: adenine (A), uracil (U) replaces thymine, plus C and G.

3. Strandedness & shape  
   • DNA: usually double-stranded helix, long and stable.  
   • RNA: usually single-stranded; can fold into complex shapes.

4. Stability  
   • DNA: chemically more stable, designed for long-term genetic storage.  
   • RNA: 2′-OH makes it less stable and more prone to hydrolysis—suited for short-term roles.

5. Primary roles  
   • DNA: permanent repository of genetic information.  
   • RNA: multiple temporary roles—messenger RNA (mRNA), transfer RNA (tRNA), ribosomal RNA (rRNA), regulatory RNAs, etc.

6. Location in eukaryotic cells  
   • DNA: confined to nucleus (and mitochondria/chloroplasts).  
   • RNA: synthesized in nucleus but functions mainly in cytoplasm; some stay in nucleus or organelles.

7. Replication vs. transcription  
   • DNA self-replicates during cell division.  
   • RNA is produced from DNA templates by transcription; it is not self-replicating (except in some viruses).

Bottom line: DNA is the durable, double-stranded archival blueprint; RNA is the versatile, single-stranded working copy and molecular toolset.
